Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (literally “from what follows”).
Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese abóbora, from Hispanic Medieval Latin apoperes of uncertain origin. Cognate of Spanish abobra and Galician abóbora.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós), from Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía, the location where Plato taught).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin accessōrius.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin accidentālis. By surface analysis, acidente + -al.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós, Catalan adeu, Dutch ajuus, English, French, and Occitan adieu, German tschüss, Greek αντίο (antío), Galician adeus, Italian addio, Maltese addiju, Mirandese adius, Romanian adio, Serbo-Croa
Borrowed from Medieval Latin admissibilis, which was based on Old French admissible, or formed from the root of Latin admissus with the suffix -ível.

parole.significato: to calibrate, to benchmark, to check the accuracy of
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *afferere, from Latin afferre.
From Medieval Latin albinus, from Latin albus.

parole.significato: alkanet (Alkanna tinctoria, a plant whose root is used as a red dye)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcanna, from Arabic الحِنَّاء (al-ḥinnāʔ).

parole.significato: place (numeric: the column counting a certain quantity)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, a transliteration of the Arabic form of the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwārizmī. Doublet of algoritmo. Cognate with Spanish guarismo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese almirante, from Medieval Latin amiratus under influence from -ante and Arabic ال (al-, “the, of the”), from Byzantine Greek ἀμιράς (amirás), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander”). See Spanish almirante, French amiral, and English admiral.

parole.significato: alternative (one of a set of mutually exclusive choices)
parole.testo: From alternativo (“alternative”), from Medieval Latin alternātīvus.

parole.significato: ambidextrous (having equal ability in both hands)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ambidexter, from Latin ambi- + dexter.

parole.significato: concubine (a woman who lives with a man, but who is not a wife)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amāsia, from Latin amāsius.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin amygdala. Doublet of amêndoa and mandorla.

parole.significato: Anglican (relating to one of several churches)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Anglicānus, suggested in the Magna Carta by Anglicana ecclesia (“the English church”), from Latin Anglicus, from Angli, Anglus (“an Englishman”). Compare anglo.
Literally, “year of Christ”. ellipsis of ano de Nosso Senhor Jesus Cristo. Ultimately from Medieval Latin annō Dominī nostrī Iēsū Christī. Compare Spanish año de Cristo.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin antiphonārium (“antiphonary”), from antiphōna (“antiphon”), from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”). By surface analysis, antífona + -ário.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin antimonium.

parole.significato: antiperistasis (the heightening of the force of an opposing process)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin antiperistasis, from Ancient Greek ἀντιπερίστασις (antiperístasis).
From Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “verse response”), from ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “responsive”), from ἀντί (antí, “against, in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).

Borrowed from Medieval Latin antithesis (“opposition, contraction”) (in Classical Latin, "permutation of letters"), from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis, “opposition”). By surface analysis, anti- + tese.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin annuitātem, from Latin annuus (“annual”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin analogus, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλογος (análogos, “proportionate”), from ἀνά (aná, “up to”) + λόγος (lógos, “ratio”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperitīvus, from Late Latin apertīvus, from Latin aperiō.

parole.significato: apothecary (person who makes or sells medicines)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin apothēcārius. Doublet of boticário.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin apothegma, from Ancient Greek ἀπόφθεγμα (apóphthegma).
From Medieval Latin apprehensīvus, from apprehensus, perfect passive participle of apprehendō (“to apprehend, understand, learn”) + -īvus (“-ive”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin aptitūdinem.
From armar + -ada (or the feminine past participle of armar), corresponding to Medieval Latin armāta, from the feminine past participle of Latin armāre, from arma (“arms”). Cf. also Italian armata.
From Medieval Latin mūs Armenius (“Armenian mouse”).

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin armistitium, from Latin arma (“weapons”) and statio (“immobility”) (compare solstitium). Cognate to Galician and Spanish armisticio, French and English armistice, Italian armistizio, Catalan armistici.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin asēitātis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin assistentia. By surface analysis, assistir + -ência.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin absedium, from Classical Latin obsīdium.
From Medieval Latin astrolabium, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “to take”).

parole.significato: activity (something done as an action or a movement)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin āctīvitātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin āctuāre (“actuate”), from Latin āctus, perfect passive participle of agō (“do, act”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin authenticāre. By surface analysis, autêntico + -ar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin auctōrizāre.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós, “original, genuine, principal”), from αὐθέντης (authéntēs, “one acting by his own authority, perpetrator, ruler”), from αὐτός (autós, “self”).
From Medieval Latin avunculāris, from Classical Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -āris (“-ar”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azur (“blue”), a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lazulum, borrowed from Arabic لََازُوَرْد (laāzuward). Doublet of azur, from French. Compare with Galician azul (“blue”), Spanish azul (“blue”), French azur (“azure”), Italian azzurro (“blue”) and English a
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin *bastōnārius (“stick-carrier”). Compare French bâtonnier.

parole.significato: to beatify (take step in declaring a person a saint)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin beātificāre (“to bless”). By surface analysis, beato + -ificar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium, from Latin bēstia.

parole.significato: pharmacist; chemist (professional who dispenses pharmaceutical drugs)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin apothēcārius. By surface analysis, botica + -ário. Doublet of apotecário.
From Medieval Latin botanicus, from Ancient Greek βοτανικός (botanikós).

parole.significato: bronchopneumonia (bacterial infection of the lungs, characteristically showing numerous small foci of infection)
parole.testo: From bronco- + pneumonia, itself from Medieval Latin pneumonia, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía), from πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”) + -ία (-ía).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal, sealed document; bull”), from Latin bulla (“bubble, rounded object”). Doublet of bola and bolha.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese burges, from Medieval Latin burgēnsis, from Latin burgus + -ēnsis. Equivalent to burgo + -ês and piecewise doublet of burguense. Compare Galician and Spanish burgués, Catalan burgès, French bourgeois and Italian borghese.
From Bósnia (“Bosnia”), from Medieval Latin Bosna (“the Bosna river”), from Latin Bossina.
From Medieval Latin Bulgarus, from Ottoman Turkish بولغار (bulgar). Doublet of bugre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin calandra, from Ancient Greek κάλανδρα (kálandra), κάλανδρος (kálandros, “lark”), from Pre-Greek or Anatolian.
From Medieval Latin camaeus. Ultimate origin unknown.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin campānārius, from campāna (“bell”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin campanula.

From Old Galician-Portuguese capela (“chapel”), from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappella (“little cloak; chapel”), diminutive of cappa (“cloak, cape”). Cognate with Galician capela, Spanish capilla, Catalan capella, Occitan capèla, French chapelle, Italian cappella and Romanian capelă.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin charactērizō, from Ancient Greek χαρακτηρίζω (kharaktērízō), from χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese celestial, a borrowing from Medieval Latin caelestiālis (“celestial”), from Latin caelestis (“celestial”), from caelum (“sky”). By surface analysis, celeste + -ial.

parole.significato: bell, cowbell (a small bell worn by cows and other animals)
parole.testo: From choca + -alho, from Old Galician-Portuguese choca, from Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”), from Gaulish *clocca, from imitative Proto-Indo-European *klak.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin scientificus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cifra (“zero, numeral”), from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “zero, empty, nothing”). Doublet of zero.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin clītoris, from Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís).
From Medieval Latin chlorosis and French chlorose. By surface analysis, cloro- + -ose.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin classicus, from Latin classicus (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis.

parole.significato: cognitive (relating to the mental functions that deals with logic)
parole.testo: From Latin cognitus + -ivo or Medieval Latin cognitīvus.

parole.significato: said of something or someone that collects
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin collectōrem, from Latin collectāre, from collectus.

parole.significato: which can be eaten without harm; comestible, edible
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin comestibilis, from Latin comedō (“to eat”). Piecewise doublet of comível.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin comitīva, from comitāre (“to accompany”).

parole.significato: to concern (to be of importance to)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin concernere (“to distinguish, to have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiōnālis (“conditional”), from conditiō (“condition”).
From Medieval Latin condomĭnus.

parole.significato: to confront (to stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

parole.significato: conjunctiva (membrane that lines the inner surface of the eyelid)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin conjūnctīva (“serving to connect, connective”, feminine), ellipsis of membrāna conjūnctīva (literally “conjunctive membrane”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiōnem, from Latin connotō. By surface analysis, conotar + -ção.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus (“convent”). By surface analysis, convento + -ual.

parole.significato: Coptic (of or relating to the Coptic people or the Coptic Orthodox Church)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin coptus.

parole.significato: choir (ensemble of people who sing together)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin chorālis. By surface analysis, coro + -al.
From Medieval Latin correspondēre.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin crēdibilitātem, from Latin credibilis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin crānium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾱνῐ́ον (krānĭ́on), from *κρᾱν- (*krān-) + -ῐ́ον (-ĭ́on).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin culmināre, from Latin culmen.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin cūrātīvus. By surface analysis, curar + -tivo.

parole.significato: handwritten (written with a pen or pencil)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin cedula.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin cōpia (“reproduction, transcript”), from Latin cōpia (“plenty, abundance”), from *coopia, from co- (“together”) + ops (“wealth, riches”).

parole.significato: church rate (amount granted to parish priests to support themselves)

From Medieval Latin decēnārius, reshaping of earlier denārius. Cognate with French décénaire, Italian decenario, Spanish decenario.

parole.significato: decisive (having the power or quality of deciding a question or controversy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēcīsīvus, from French décisif, from Latin dēcīsus.

parole.significato: dental (of or concerning teeth, cleaning teeth)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dentālis, from Latin dēns (“a tooth”). By surface analysis, dente + -al.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin depauperare (“to impoverish”), from Latin de- + pauperare (“to impoverish”), from pauper (“poor”). Cognate with Spanish depauperar, English depauperate.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēpūrāre, from pūrus (“pure”).

parole.significato: refund (of a product, being able to send the physical item back to the seller)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dēvolutiōnem, from Latin dēvolvō.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diametrālis. By surface analysis, diâmetro (“diameter”) + -al.

parole.significato: diet (food a person or animal consumes)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin dieta (“regimen, regulation; assembly”), from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita). Doublet of diet.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.

parole.significato: diplomatics (the study of old official documents)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin diplōmātica.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin disponibilis. By surface analysis, dispor + -ível.

parole.significato: the act or result of diverging (to tend into different directions)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dīversiōnem, from Latin dīversus (“opposite; apart; diverse”), past participle of dīvertō (“to divert; to separate”).

parole.significato: doxology (expression of praise to God, especially a short hymn)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”), from δοξολόγος (doxológos, “giving or uttering praise”).

parole.significato: duchy (a dominion or region ruled by a duke or duchess)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ducātus, from Latin dux.

parole.significato: dura mater (outermost layer of the meninges)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dūra māter [cerebrī] (literally “hard mother [of the brain]”), loan translation of Arabic أُمّ الدِّمَاغ الصَفِيقَة (ʔumm ad-dimāḡ aṣ-ṣafīqa, literally “thick mother of the brain, matrix of the brain”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin dūrātiōnem. By surface analysis, durar + -ção.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin effectuāre.; compare French effectuer, Italian effettuare, Spanish and Catalan efectuar. From Latin effectus, perfect passive participle of efficiō (“to effect, to execute, to complete, to accomplish”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin embryon, from Ancient Greek ἔμβρυον (émbruon, “fetus”), from ἐν (en, “in-”) + βρύω (brúō, “to grow, to swell”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmergentia, from Latin ēmergentem. By surface analysis, emergir + -ência.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin entem.

parole.significato: entity (something or somebody that exists as an individual unit)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin entitātem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aequilībrāre (“to weigh out, to apportion”), from Latin aequilībris (“of the same weight, in balance”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin aequivalentia.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Erasmiānus, from Erasmus. By surface analysis, Erasmo + -iano.

parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Medieval Latin Erasmus. Doublet of Erasmo.

From Medieval Latin sparadrapum, of obscure origin. Compare Spanish esparadrapo, Catalan esparadrap, French sparadrap, Italian sparadrappo, Sicilian sparatrappu.
From Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).

parole.significato: to stigmatize (to characterize as disgraceful or ignominious)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stigmatizō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin oesophagus, from Ancient Greek οἰσοφάγος (oisophágos).
From Medieval Latin excentricus, from ex- (“away”) + centrum (“centre”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin exemplificāre, from Latin exemplum (“example”). By surface analysis, exemplo + -ificar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin extrāvagantem.

parole.significato: to exhume (to take out of a place of burial)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin exhumāre, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

parole.significato: fallible (capable of making mistakes or being wrong)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallō (“to deceive, trick, cheat, disappoint”). By surface analysis, falir + -ível.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharyngem, borrowed from Ancient Greek φάρυγξ (phárunx, “throat, gullet”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bʰruHg-, *bʰerH-, or Pre-Greek *?.

parole.significato: a cabinet where medicine is stored
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”), from φάρμακον (phármakon, “a drug, charm, enchantment”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris. By surface analysis, febre + -il.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin fīlāmentum, from Late Latin fīlō (“to spin, draw out in a long line”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin flamencus, from Old Dutch flāmisk (Modern Dutch Vlaams), from Proto-Germanic *flaumaz + *-iskaz.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese frolido, a semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin flōridus, from Latin flōreō + -idus. Doublet of Flórida.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin frangibilis. By surface analysis, franger + -ível.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frāternālis (“fraternal”), from Latin frāternus (“of or relating to a brother, fraternal”), from frāter (“brother”).
From fronte (“front”) + -al (“of or relating to”), or borrowed from Medieval Latin frontālis (“frontal”), from Latin frōns.
From Medieval Latin fungibilis, from Latin fungor (“to perform, to complete”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin graduālis.

parole.significato: heretical (of or relating to heresy or heretics)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin haereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”). Doublet of herege.

parole.significato: homogeneous (of the same kind; alike, similar)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin homogeneus, from Ancient Greek ὁμογενής (homogenḗs, “of the same race, family or kind”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + γένος (génos, “kind”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin horārius, from Latin hora (“hour”) + -ārius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hungarus, from German Ungar.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin illēgālis, from Latin lēgālis. By surface analysis, i- + legal.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus.
From Medieval Latin inclusīve, from inclūsīvus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus.

parole.significato: to incriminate (to accuse or bring criminal charges against)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīmināre, from Latin crīmināre.
From Medieval Latin īnstantāneus, from Latin īnstantem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer (“entire; untouched”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intēnsīvus, from Latin intēnsus.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intimidāre (“to make afraid”), from Latin in (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”).
From Medieval Latin intromissiōnem, from Latin intrōmittō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin intuitīvus. By surface analysis, intuir + -tivo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inventīvus, from Latin inventum.

parole.significato: jugular (relating to the neck or throat)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Scientific Latin iugularis, jugularis, from Latin iugulum.

parole.significato: jurist (expert in law consulted by a court)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin iūrista.

parole.significato: labial (of or relating to the lips)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin labiālis. By surface analysis, lábio + -al.

parole.significato: to speak Latin, to understand Latin
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin latināre.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin linguālis, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech”) + -ālis. By surface analysis, língua + -al.

From lixívia, or borrowed from a Medieval Latin *lixīviāre.

parole.significato: logistic (relating to the transportation of goods or supplies)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin logisticus, from Ancient Greek λογιστικός (logistikós).
From Medieval Latin lūnātiō.

parole.significato: hop (plant whose flowers are used in ale brewing, Humulus lupulus)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin lupulus. Compare Italian luppolo and Spanish lúpulo.

parole.significato: honeysuckle (any plant of the genus Lonicera)

parole.significato: marjoram (Origanum majorana, a herb of the mint family)
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin maiōrāna.

parole.significato: metaphysician (philosopher who specializes in the scholarly study of metaphysics)
parole.testo: From metafísica (“metaphysics”), from Medieval Latin metaphysica (“metaphysics”), from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká). By surface analysis, meta- + físico.

Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin misericordiōsus. By surface analysis, misericórdia + -oso. Compare French miséricordieux.

parole.significato: morganatic (between a man of higher rank and a woman of lower rank)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin morganāticus, from Late Latin mātrimōnium ad morganāticam, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning-gift”), from *murginaz (“morning”) + *gēbǭ (“gift”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin mōtīvus.
Inherited from Medieval Latin maura.
From mover + -imento, perhaps based partly on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō, from Proto-Indo-European *m(y)ewh₁- (“to move”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin mūsicālis. By surface analysis, música + -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin maxima.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin necessitāre, from Latin necessitās.
Perhaps from Medieval Latin nichil (“nothing”).
Ultimately borrowed from Medieval Latin nichil, from Latin nihil.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius.

parole.significato: occurrence (actual instance where a situation arises)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin occurrentia. By surface analysis, ocorrer + -ência.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin offēnsīvus, from Latin offēnsus, past participle of offendō (“to offend”). By surface analysis, ofenso + -ivo.

parole.significato: offering (object given to a person or sacrificed to a god in order to appease them)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin offerenda, from Latin offerendus. Compare French offrande, Catalan ofrena, Spanish ofrenda.

parole.significato: offer (a proposal that has been made)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese offerta, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Catalan and Spanish oferta, Italian offerta.
From Medieval Latin oleandru, from Late Latin lorandrum, perhaps an alteration of rhododendron.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin omniscientem (“all-knowing”), from omni- (“all”) + sciēns (“knowing”) (compare Portuguese ciente (“aware”)).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin omniscientia (“all-knowledge”), from omni- (“all”) + scientia (“knowledge”) (compare Portuguese ciência (“science”)).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin onagra, from Ancient Greek ὀνάγρα (onágra).

parole.significato: ordeal (trial in which the accused was subjected to a dangerous test)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ordālium.
From paliar (“to palliate”) + -tivo (“-ive”), from Medieval Latin palliāre (“to cloak”), from Latin pallium (“a cloak”).

parole.significato: papal (related to the pope or papacy)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin papālis. By surface analysis, papa + -al.

parole.significato: paroxysm (a random or sudden outburst of activity)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin partītīvus, from Latin partītus + -īvus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese pendurar, pendorar, from Medieval Latin pendulāre, from Latin pendulus (“hanging”), from pendeō (“to hang”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin penetrābilis. By surface analysis, penetrar + -ável.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin perspectīva (“science of optics”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin petroleum, from Latin petra (“rock”) + oleum (“oil”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese peon, an early semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pedōnem (“one who goes on foot”), from Latin pēs (“foot”). Compare Galician peón, Spanish peón, French pion, Italian pedone.

parole.significato: pia mater (innermost layer of the meninges)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pia māter (literally “tender mother”).
From Medieval Latin pyramidalis. By surface analysis, pirâmide + -al.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pneumonia, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía).
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis. By surface analysis, ponto + -ual.

parole.significato: punctuality (state or quality of being punctual, on time)
parole.testo: From pontual (“punctual”) + -idade (“-ity”), from Medieval Latin pūnctuālis (“having a sharp point”), from Latin pūnctum (“point”), from pungō (“to prick, to puncture, to punch”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin posse (“power, ability”).

parole.significato: to postpone (to delay or put off an event for later)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin postergāre, from Latin post (“after”) + tergum (“back, back side”).

parole.significato: beach (shore of a body of water, especially when sandy or pebbly)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese praia, from Medieval Latin plagia, possibly from Latin plaga + Ancient Greek πλάγια (plágia). Doublet of plaga. Cognate with Galician praia, Sicilian praja, Spanish playa, Catalan platja, Occitan plaja, French plage and Italian spiaggia.

parole.significato: to practice (repeat an activity as a way of improving one’s skill)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin prāctica (“practical affairs; business”), from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτική (prāktikḗ, “practice, experience”), from πρακτικός (praktikós, “practical”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”).

parole.significato: predicament (a definite class, state or condition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedicāmentum, derived from Latin praedicō (“to declare, proclame, predicate”).

parole.significato: preamble (introduction to a formal document or statute)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Late Latin praeambulō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin prioritātem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese promessa, from Medieval Latin, Vulgar Latin prōmissa (“promise”), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

parole.significato: tuition, a fee for services such as enrollment or obtaining a document
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin propīna. Compare Italian and Spanish propina.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōpulsiōnem, from Latin prōpulsus.

parole.significato: prosaic (pertaining to or having the characteristics of prose)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōsaicus (“in prose”), from Latin prōsa (“prose”).
From Medieval Latin prostata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pūblicitātem, derived from Latin pūblicus (“public, general”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quālificāre. By surface analysis, qual + -ificar.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quālificātiōnem. By surface analysis, qualificar + -ção.

parole.significato: quintal, a nonstandard unit of mass equal to 100 kg
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quintāle (“various medieval hundredweights”), from Andalusian Arabic and Arabic قِنْطَار (qinṭār, “100 rottols”), from Classical Syriac ܩܰܢܛܺܝܪܳܐ (qanṭīrā) and ܩܰܢܛܺܝܢܳܪܳܐ (qanṭīnārā), from Byzantine Greek κεντηνάριον (kentēnárion), from Latin centēnārium (“100 Roman pounds”). Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rāmificāre (“to branch, ramify”). By surface analysis, ramo + -ificar.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificāre, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin receptīvus, from Latin receptus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin remorsus, from Latin remordeō (“to torment, to vex”, literally “to bite back”) from re- + mordeō (“to bite”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin repulsīvus, from Latin repulsus. Compare French répulsif.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).
From Medieval Latin respectīvus, from Latin respectus (compare respeito).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin resultāre, frequentative of classical Latin resilīre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin retorta, from Latin retortus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin or Late Latin rectangulum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin reversibilis. From Latin reversus + -ibilis. Piecewise doublet of revertível.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin rotātōrius, from Classical Latin rotō.
From Old Galician-Portuguese roubo, from roubar, from Medieval Latin raubāre from Proto-Germanic *raubōną.

parole.significato: sacristan (an individual who is in charge of the arrangement of the sacristy or a church)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sacristānus.
From Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).

parole.significato: secretary (a person keeping records and handling clerical work)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius (“secretary”), from Latin sēcrētus, perfect passive participle of sēcernō (“to separate; to part; to reject”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sinus (“sine”), from Latin sinus (“curve, breast”). Doublet of seio and sino.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sēnsātiōnem, from Latin sēnsus.
From Medieval Latin syringa, from sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx). Doublet of siringe.
From Medieval Latin seraphicus.
From the Medieval Latin simplificārī. By surface analysis, simples + -ificar.

parole.significato: signet (object (especially a ring) used to impress a picture into sealing wax)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin signētum, diminutive of Latin signum.
From Medieval Latin Sina (“China”), from Latin Sinae (“the Southern Chinese; Southern China”), from Ancient Greek Σῖναι (Sînai), q.v.

parole.significato: sorority (a sororal group composed exclusively of females)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sorōritātem, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. By surface analysis, soror + -idade. Akin to Spanish sororidad, French sororité, English sorority.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin sortilegium, from Latin sortilegus (“sorcerer, diviner”), from sors (“sort”) + legere (“choose”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin subōrdināre, from Latin sub- + ōrdinō (“to sort, to order”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin superiōritātem, from Latin superior. By surface analysis, superior (“superior”) + -idade.
From suplir, from Medieval Latin supplēre. Compare English supply, French suppléer, Italian supplire and Spanish suplir.
From Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy).
From Medieval Latin thaumaturgus, from Ancient Greek θαυματουργός (thaumatourgós).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese taxar, a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin taxāre.

parole.significato: key (button on a typewriter or computer keyboard)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin thēcula, diminutive of Latin thēca (“box”), perhaps blended with a descendant of Latin tēgula (“tile”).

parole.significato: tendon (tissue that connects a muscle with a bone)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin tendō, tendōnem, from Ancient Greek τένων (ténōn, “sinew, tendon”)
Borrowed from Medieval Latin terraqueus.

parole.significato: writing (written letters or symbols that express some meaning)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese texto, borrowed from Medieval Latin textus (“text”), from Latin textus (“woven”), perfect passive participle of texō (“weave”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin textuālis. By surface analysis, texto + -ual.
From Medieval Latin thōrācicus, from Ancient Greek θωρακικός (thōrakikós, “suffering in the chest, of the thorax”), from θώραξ (thṓrax, “thorax”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin tōtālis (“total”), from Latin tōtus (“whole”) + -ālis (“-al”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), from trānspāreō, from Latin trāns + pāreō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānspārentia, from trānspārēns (“transparent”).

parole.significato: to perspire, to sweat (to emit sweat)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin trānspīrāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin trānspīrātiōnem, from trānspīrō, from Latin trāns + spīrō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tractiōnem, from Latin tractus.

parole.significato: to replace, to substitute (to remove something and put a new one in its place)
parole.testo: First used in the 14th century, from Old Galician-Portuguese trocar, from Medieval Latin trocāre; further etymology uncertain (probably Frankish *trokōn). Cognate with Spanish, Galician, Catalan, and Occitan trocar, French troquer, English truck.

parole.significato: change (small denominations of money given in exchange for a larger denomination)
parole.testo: Deverbal from trocar (“to switch; to exchange”), from Medieval Latin trocāre (“to barter”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tregua, from Medieval Latin tregua, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *trewwō, possibly Proto-West Germanic *treuwu, or possibly Gothic 𐍄𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌲𐍅𐌰 (triggwa). Cognate with truce.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese turquo, from Medieval Latin Turcus, borrowed from Byzantine Greek Τοῦρκος (Toûrkos), borrowed from Classical Persian ترک, from Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰜 (t²ẅr²ẅk²), from Proto-Turkic *tür(ü)k.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tartaro, from Medieval Latin Tartarus (“Tatar”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ūrīnāre. By surface analysis, urina + -ar.
From Medieval Latin usufructus, shortening of the Latin phrase usus et fructus.

From Medieval Latin vāna glōria, from Latin vāna (“empty, groundless, boastful”) + glōria (“fame, ambition, boasting”). By surface analysis, vã (“vain”) + glória (“glory”). Cognate with English vainglory, Italian and Spanish vanagloria.

parole.significato: Varangian (member of a Scandinavian tribe that settled around Constantinople)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Varingus, from Old Norse væringi.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese vassalo, from Medieval Latin vassallus (“manservant, domestic, retainer”), from vassus (“servant”), from Gaulish *wassos (“young man, squire”), from Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”) (compare Old Irish foss and Welsh gwas).

parole.significato: vegetable (edible material derived from a plant)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetālis, from Latin vegetō.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vegetativus. Compare French végétatif.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin vērificāre. By surface analysis, vero + -ificar. Doublet of averiguar.

parole.significato: varnish (type of paint that leaves a hard, glossy film)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese verniz, a borrowing from Medieval Latin vernīcem (“varnish”) < veronīx, from Byzantine Greek, from Ancient Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē, “a city in Lybia”).
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin versiōnem.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin vestuārium, corruption of Latin vestiārium, from vestis (“clothing”).

parole.significato: virtual (in effect or essence, not in fact or reality)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin virtuālis.

parole.significato: viscount (a member of the nobility above a baron but below a count)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin vice-comitis.
From Medieval Latin volitiōnem, based on Latin volō (“to want”).
From Medieval Latin cibōrium (“drinking cup”). Compare Portuguese cibório and English ciborium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ebanus, from Italian ebano influencing Latin (h)ebenus, ultimately from Egyptian.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin epocha, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ).

parole.significato: pirate; corsair (one who plunders at sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian corsaro, from Medieval Latin cursārius. Alternatively, reformed from earlier cossário and cossairo as corso + -ário.

parole.significato: engineer (person qualified or professionally engaged in engineering)
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin ingeniārius (“one who makes or uses an engine”), composed of inherited engenho + -eiro, from Latin ingenium (“an engine”). Alternatively a calque of French ingénieur composed in the same fashion. Compare also Spanish ingeniero.

From Old French escarlate (“scarlet cloth”), from Medieval Latin scarlatum (“scarlet cloth”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Persian سقرلاط (saqerlât, “a warm woollen cloth”), a variant of سقلاط (seqellât, “scarlet cloth”), from Byzantine Greek σιγιλλᾶτος (sigillâtos), ultimately from Latin

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese faisca, feisca (attested in Medieval Latin as falisca), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *falwiskǭ (“spark, ash over burning ambers”), from Proto-Germanic *falwaz (“fallow”) from Proto-Indo-European *polʷos, or from Vulgar Latin *favillesca, from favilla
Borrowed from French macle, either from Latin macula (from Italic) or from Medieval Latin mascula (from Germanic); see French and English macle for more.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from para- + fuso, from Medieval Latin *pare fusu or from Spanish parahúso.
Borrowed from French rime, from Old French rime; or from Medieval Latin rhythmus.
